extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, geometers, and advanced students interested in diagrammatic reasoning and mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of the roles, limits, and standards governing diagram use in traditional Euclidean geometrical practice, including case distinctions, construction determinateness, and diagram-based reductio. Focuses on how diagrams and discursive text jointly license inferences and control possible diagrammatic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness (or finite-variant) of geometric constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric constructions purport to give unique outcomes, or outcomes unique up to finitely many variants in any given case (e.g., the line connecting two points is unique; the equilateral triangle construction I.1 gives two congruent but differently located triangles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize uniqueness as either strict uniqueness or quasi-uniqueness (finitely many legitimate outcomes). Some Euclidean propositions (e.g., I.7) address uniqueness explicitly; where not explicit, diagram discipline and practice supply the expectation of uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-propositional acquaintance with control in executing constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary resource: a non-propositional grasp that certain constructions, when properly executed in a diagram, have no legitimately competing alternate outcomes (part of what must be undertaken under Postulate 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This attenuated, inarticulate sense of uniqueness is operative in practice and compatible with Euclid's lack of explicit propositional claims about uniqueness. Practitioners must be able to 'grasp' appropriate control when making diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-determinateness: finitely many outcomes and corresponding conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A determinate construction has at most finitely many outcomes; each outcome corresponds to an independently intelligible geometrical condition on initial data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metatheoretical means can establish finiteness of outcomes; practice must be sensitive to which initial-data conditions yield which outcomes even when practitioners cannot read off those conditions from a single diagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for propositionally explicit claims when diagram-grasp is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: When non-propositional (diagram-based) grasp cannot reveal which outcomes occur (e.g., close-to-threshold cases), the practice relies on propositionally explicit claims and demonstrations regarding outcomes (e.g., uniqueness results like I.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift from purely diagram-based moves to mixed diagram-and-text demonstrations to settle ambiguous or metrically sensitive outcome questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective uniqueness via treating a single outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional practice often treats one outcome (provided its standing is not in question) and leaves it to probing to see if other outcome-diagrams produce something different; this gamble reduces quasi-uniqueness to effective uniqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating a single outcome is acceptable as a pragmatic device, but practitioners implicitly accept vulnerability to overlooked alternatives; subsequent probing may expose alternate outcomes that require further argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinateness extends beyond uniqueness (appearance & metric data)
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinateness import of constructions is not exhausted by uniqueness/existence: knowing a construction gives a unique result need not determine the metric properties or appearance of the result-diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagram discipline typically handles appearance issues, but extreme-sensitivity cases (e.g., arbitrarily close-to-isoceles triangles) may exceed diagrammatic control; awareness of this limitation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stipulative diagram control (resolving artifact-range ambiguities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some diagram-appearance problems can be resolved by stipulation (e.g., different ways to interpret the 'intersection too far to draw' lead to Euclidean, hyperbolic, elliptic, or projective stipulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stipulative resolutions are possible but raise questions about whether the practice independently controls appearance so as to render the stipulation superfluous or incompatible; such stipulations must remain compatible with core practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case distinctions driven by diagram topology
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional geometrical reasoning distinguishes many cases because diagrams individuate claims and proofs; when capacity for uniform proceeding fails (in a finite-to-one way) one must enumerate cases (Apollonius example: ~87 cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when topological changes (a point passing from one side of a line to another, tangency vs intersection, etc.) force separate treatments. Omitting necessary cases risks disarray in proofs and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: One appearance–one diagram principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Topologically distinct diagrams are treated in separate argument; diagrams with the same appearance should not be treated separately if the appearance is the same—i.e., 'one appearance–one diagram'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appearance/topology of diagrams to individuate claims and proofs; this provides a local optimum between managing diversity of spatial forms and retaining inferential grip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discursive text as a resource for uniformity across cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric text (discursive representation) can give the appearance of greater uniformity of presentation than diagram-based demonstration, allowing formulation uniformity that diagrams cannot sustain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may substitute separate discursive claims (p1→q) and (p2→q) for diagrammatic case splits, or use text to describe appearance conditions more fully. But text is still constrained by diagram-based inferences when those are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case branching from further constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Topologically similar initial diagrams may become dissimilar after auxiliary constructions; when this happens the proof must handle the different resulting diagrams separately (case branching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that added constructions can change topology; proofs should branch when uniform proceeding after the construction falls short of prior uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustiveness requirement for appearances in arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof is to be applicable to any diagram meeting the proposition's stated conditions, precisely those appearances which might arise in the argument should be presented, one diagram each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should, where practicable, present each potentially relevant appearance; in practice, authors differ in completeness, and some immaterial appearance differences can be omitted once argument structure is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: no general procedure to certify completeness or generate case variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional practice lacks procedures either to certify completeness of case distinctions or to generate variant diagrams; free metric choices and relationships between those choices and appearance are generally unsurveyable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that diagrams come one at a time and that making one set of choices yields little grasp of the full range of alternative outcomes; this limitation constrains the capacity to ensure exhaustive case coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus descriptions as a partial survey tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain locus descriptions (e.g., locus of points making a fixed angle is a circle) give a limited survey of all possible placements satisfying a condition and help read off some interactions with other diagram elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use locus results to gain partial, structured information about families of possibilities; they still may not allow comprehensive enumeration or prevent cluttering the diagram if multiple instances are drawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram-based reductio requires hypothesis convertible into diagram conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: To proceed by reductio in a diagram-based argument, the hypothesis for reductio (C1&...&Cn&¬D) must be convertible into diagram conditions: ¬D typically must be expressible as inequalities or proper-part relations readable in the diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negations often convert via trichotomy into disjunctions of strict inequalities, and inequalities into proper-part relations using auxiliary equalities; success of reductio depends on this convertibility (I.6 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer conjunctive single-diagram hypotheses for reductio
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductio works best when the hypothesis forms a conjunctive system of conditions concerning a single diagram rather than a disjunction of variant diagrams—disjunctive hypotheses produce exponential case explosions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid starting diagram-based reductio from an inarticulate denial (¬(D1&...&Dm)) that cannot be converted into diagram conditions; such starting points are poor for diagram-based reductio and likely impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of move-licensing between diagram and discursive text
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can be unaffected by diagrammatic incompatibility between premises and the denial of the conclusion provided responsibility for licensing moves is divided so that it is indifferent whether the diagram exhibits all exact textual conditions (example: Euclid I.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable for the diagram to lack some exact metric equalities so long as those equalities are asserted in the discursive text and the diagram supplies the topological/co-exact conditions needed to read off the inferential moves; critics can then propose variants to test standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and conventions in subjecting diagrams to exact conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a diagram cannot be subjected to all exact conditions of the discursive text, there is a practice of prioritizing which exact conditions to subject—often those indicated earlier in the text—and treating equivalent items equivalently in the diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions include breaking or curving segments to indicate intersections or to preserve parity among equivalent elements; choice of which exact conditions to depict follows textual order and perceived role-equivalence in the argument.
